Participants had a mean age of 41.8 years with a wide variability in symptom severity. Their main concerns were retaining self-agency, combating stigma, and leaning into hope and positivity. While valuing decision-making autonomy, they recognized that MS can complicate EOL decision-making. Participants looked to family and health care providers for cues about cognitive changes and found that hope and positivity provided comfort as the disease progressed. Understanding participants' perspectives will help clinicians support individuals as they navigate their disease trajectory during EOL care planning, will help policy makers enhance the health care system to ensure EOL care accessibility for the MS community, and support individual choice for people with MS.

title: Domain-Specific Cognitive Associations With Standing Balance in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Balance impairments and cognitive deficits are both prevalent in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS) and contribute to elevated fall risk. Although prior studies have examined global cognition and balance, few have investigated the relation between specific cognitive domains and balance performance under progressively challenging static conditions. Fifty-four ambulatory individuals with MS completed 4 standing balance tasks that increased in difficulty by altering visual input (eyes open/closed) and stance (feet apart/together). Sway velocity was measured using inertial sensors. Participants also completed assessments of processing speed (Symbol Digit Modalities Test [SDMT]), attention and cognitive flexibility (Trail Making Test parts A [TMT-A] and B), verbal and visuospatial memory (California Verbal Learning Test, Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised), and concern about falling (Falls Efficacy Scale-International [FES-I]). Spearman correlations and linear regressions, adjusted for age, sex, and disability level, were used to examine associations between cognitive/psychological variables and balance performance. Processing speed (SDMT) was significantly associated with sway during the least complex condition (eyes open, feet apart). Under more challenging conditions (eyes closed), attention (TMT-A) and concern about falling (FES-I) emerged as significant predictors of balance performance. They remained significant after adjusting for disability level. Domain-specific cognitive performance and concern about falling are associated with postural control in people with MS, particularly under sensory-conflicting conditions. These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of balance impairment in MS and suggest that cognitive and psychological assessments may aid in identifying individuals at increased fall risk.

title: Real-World Classification of Pain States in Multiple Sclerosis Patients using Wearable Sensor Data and Ensemble Machine Learning.
abstract: Pain assessment remains challenging due to its subjective nature and reliance on self-reports. These challenges are particularly relevant for multiple sclerosis (MS) patients, for whom pain is among the most common and fluctuating symptoms, occurring in multiple forms. Wearable sensors combined with machine learning (ML) offer the potential for continuous and more objective pain monitoring by leveraging physiological signals in real-world contexts. We monitored 18 MS patients over 48 h using the Empatica E4 wristband to collect photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometer data. Physiological features were extracted from 5-, 10-, and 15-min time windows preceding hourly self-reported pain assessment during waking hours. Univariate associations with pain states were evaluated using linear mixed effects models, correcting for multiple comparisons. For classification purposes, feature selection was performed via recursive feature elimination, and 5 ML algorithms were trained and tested with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using the F1 score and the sensitivity-specificity balance. For univariate analysis, after correction, only 2 out of 43 features showed significant differences between pain and no-pain states. For the classification task, models based on 5-min windows generally performed the best. The highest F1 score (0.78) was achieved by a Support Vector Machine using 2 features from 5-min windows, while XGBoost achieved the best sensitivity-specificity balance (0.69/0.68) with 2 features from 15-min windows. Wearable physiological signals may contain information relevant to pain-state classification in people with MS. However, these results should be considered preliminary, requiring validation in larger, independent cohorts to establish the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach.

title: Rebound-Like Inflammatory Activity Presenting as a Tumefactive Demyelinating Lesion after Teriflunomide Discontinuation: A Case Report.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rebound after teriflunomide discontinuation is uncommon and difficult to distinguish from ordinary disease reactivation without a documented pretreatment baseline. Tumefactive demyelination is a rarely reported post-cessation phenotype. CASE PRESENTATION: This report presents a 39-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis had no relapses, Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) worsening, or new MRI lesions during approximately 5 years of teriflunomide treatment. She stopped treatment without medical supervision or an accelerated elimination procedure for pregnancy planning. Four months later, persistent headache prompted MRI, which showed a 2.6 × 2.6-cm right frontal periventricular tumefactive demyelinating lesion with edema, peripheral diffusion restriction, and mild ring enhancement, plus a new left cerebellar plaque. EDSS remained 0. Absolute lymphocyte count rose from 600 cells/μL at the last on-treatment visit to 1,700 cells/μL at presentation. Serum MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG and CSF cytology were negative; a type 2 oligoclonal-band pattern was present, and targeted infectious screening showed no evidence of active infection. Teriflunomide concentration was <0.02 mg/L twice, 14 days apart. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) resolved the headache. Cladribine was then started, and 1-month MRI showed marked regression. EDSS remained 0 and no new or enhancing lesion appeared through 12 months. CONCLUSION: The tumor-like lesion exceeded the patient's pretreatment radiological phenotype, but the absence of objective deficit, EDSS worsening, and a high lesion burden makes definitive rebound uncertain. Rebound-like post-cessation inflammatory activity is the most defensible description. Supervised treatment transition and clinical and MRI monitoring are important when teriflunomide is stopped.

title: Physical and psychological burden in RRMS: depression and fatigue beyond disease duration.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, autoimmune, demyelinating and neurodegenerative disease. Accumulation of physical and psychological disabilities adversely affects patients' health-related quality of life. The 29-item Multiple Sclerosis Impact Scale (MSIS-29) is a self-reported measure of the physical and psychological burden. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the physical and psychological impact levels in patients with MS and to examine their relationship with disease duration. METHODS: We enrolled 100 consecutive adults aged 18 to 55 years with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS). The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), annual relapse rate (ARR), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), MSIS-29, and Timed 25-Foot Walk Test (25-FWT) were applied. RESULTS: A total of 57 participants (57%) were female patients. The mean age was 38.5 ± 8.0 years, and the mean disease duration, 9.8 ± 6.8 years. The mean MSIS-29 physical and psychological scores were 36.7 ± 15.7 and 45.3 ± 20.4 respectively. No significant differences were found between patients with disease duration ≤ 10 and > 10 years in terms of the physical (p = 0.263) or psychological (p = 0.551) subscales. Physical impact was significantly associated with the female sex (p = 0.021) and the scpres on the EDSS (p = 0.030), BDI (p < 0.001), and FSS (p < 0.001). Psychological impact showed significant associations with the female sex (p = 0.005), ARR (p = 0.020), and the scores on the BDI (p < 0.001), and FSS (p < 0.001). On multivariate regression, the scores on the EDSS, BDI, and 25-FWT were independent predictors of physical impact, while the female sex and the scores on the EDSS and BDI were independent predictors of psychological impact. CONCLUSION: Disease duration did not predict physical or psychological impact in RRMS. Depression severity, lower-extremity function, and the female sex were the independent determinants of disease-related impact in the multivariate analysis. The association of fatigue with disease impact, significant at the bivariate level, was attenuated by depression in the multivariate analysis. Routine assessment of these modifiable factors should be accompanied by disease-modifying treatments in MS care.

title: Menopause and Neurology: Clinical Essentials.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Menopause is a neurobiological transition with important implications for neurologic care. This review summarizes the physiology and hormonal changes of spontaneous menopause and its treatment as applied to cognition, epilepsy, migraine, multiple sclerosis (MS), and stroke. It aims to serve as a resource for neurologists when managing patients in this transitional life stage. RECENT FINDINGS: Hormonal shifts associated with menopause, particularly declining estrogen and fluctuating estrogen-to-progesterone ratios, influence symptoms, disease expression, and treatment across multiple neurologic conditions. Perimenopause is often associated with subjective cognitive complaints, in part attributed to hypoestrogenism, along with secondary effects from sleep disturbance, vasomotor symptoms, and mood changes. Cognitive symptoms are often transient and rarely with objective neuropsychological deficits or progression. In epilepsy, menopause-related endogenous and exogenous hormones may influence seizure susceptibility and alter antiseizure medication metabolism. Migraine may worsen during perimenopause, especially in estrogen-sensitive phenotypes, with postmenopause stabilization once hormones plateau. In MS, perimenopause and postmenopause contribute to overlapping age-related and MS-related symptoms and is a period of high clinical need with potential acceleration in disability progression despite reduced relapse rate. Ischemic stroke risk rises sharply in postmenopausal women driven by advancing age, accumulation of cardiometabolic risk, and loss of estrogen's protective effects. Oral estrogen-containing systemic menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is associated with increased thromboembolic events (including stroke), whereas transdermal regimens seem safer and are preferred at low or standard doses (≤50 mcg estradiol patch or ≤1.5 mg [or 2 pumps] per day of 0.06% estradiol gel). Timing of initiation also modulates this risk and plays a critical role with a favorable risk:benefit window when initiated in women younger than 60 years or within 10 years of menopause onset. SUMMARY: Neurologists should routinely consider reproductive history, menopausal stage, symptom burden, and disease risk factors when evaluating midlife and older female patients. When appropriately selected, MHT can be safely used in many neurologic populations, with nonoral routes for estrogen and nonhormonal options generally preferred. Incorporating menopausal considerations into neurologic practice offers an important opportunity to optimize care and advance precision medicine.

title: The impact of rising global temperatures on neurological diseases.
abstract: Climate change, driven predominantly by anthropogenic actions, represents a defining challenge of the 21st century. While its general health implications are well documented, the specific impact of global warming on neurological diseases has remained underemphasized for decades. To evaluate the association between rising global temperatures and the exacerbation or incidence of various neurological conditions through a systematic review. A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed/MEDLINE and SciELO databases for studies published between 2011 and 2026. Following strict eligibility criteria, 13 peer-reviewed articles were selected for qualitative synthesis. The evidence reveals that rising temperatures are increasingly linked to the worsening of conditions such as epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Specifically, heat exposure is associated with higher hospitalization rates and acute symptom exacerbation, such as Uhthoff's phenomenon in MS and autonomic thermoregulatory failure in Parkinson's. Although some geographic and methodological discrepancies exist, particularly regarding stroke and seizure frequency, the overall trend indicates increased neurological vulnerability to thermal stress. While research is expanding, neurological diseases remain an understudied frontier of the climate crisis. Targeted scientific investigation and robust public health strategies are imperative to mitigate the emerging neurological risks of a warming planet.

title: Cryptic Presentations of Neurologic Wilson Disease With ATP7B Peptide Assessments.
abstract: To illustrate the phenotypic variability in neurologic Wilson disease (NWD) and diagnostic value of ATP7B peptide testing in resolving WD cases. We conducted a case series analysis of 3 individuals with suspected NWD. Clinical presentation, diagnostic workup including traditional biomarkers, genetic testing, and ATP7B peptide quantification by immuno-selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry were reviewed. The 3 patients demonstrated diverse neurologic presentations: (1) an adult with coexisting Parkinson disease and WD, exhibiting parkinsonian features with partial response to dopaminergic therapy; (2) a child with early-onset dystonia and neuropsychiatric symptoms; and (3) an adult initially misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. In these cases, ATP7B peptide testing revealed either markedly reduced or undetectable levels, confirming WD. These cases emphasize the diagnostic complexity of NWD. ATP7B peptide analysis via immuno-SRM-MS provided direct evidence of ATP7B protein deficiency and confirmed variant pathogenicity demonstrating its use as a rapid, noninvasive, functionally informative diagnostic adjunct. As the assay is further validated and piloted for newborn screening, it holds promise for improving early detection and clinical outcomes in WD.

title: Advanced age at onset is associated with distinct functional brain reorganization in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Functional network reorganization supports compensatory mechanisms in multiple sclerosis, but ageing and later disease onset may alter this balance. Late-onset multiple sclerosis (age at onset ≥50 years) represents a relevant subgroup to examine how disease onset in older age is associated with functional connectivity abnormalities. In this cross-sectional study, we investigated resting-state functional connectivity alterations in late-onset multiple sclerosis versus adult-onset multiple sclerosis and their associations with clinical, cognitive and structural MRI measures. Thirty-four late-onset multiple sclerosis, 169 sex- and disease duration-matched adult-onset multiple sclerosis, and 163 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent clinical, neuropsychological (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological Tests) and MRI assessment including resting-state functional MRI. Independent component analysis quantified resting-state functional connectivity within 10 large-scale networks. title: An ARG1-associated immunometabolic program in bone marrow PMN-MDSC-like cells in multiple sclerosis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Recent work indicates that bone-marrow hematopoietic niches sense CNS autoimmunity and enhance myeloid output. However, whether MS bone marrow contains an immunometabolic PMN-MDSC-like state, and whether related ARG1-associated observations can be examined in a cross-species EAE context, remains unclear. We reanalyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from treatment-naive patients with MS and healthy controls, focusing on myeloid states. We used donor-aware proportion analysis, trajectory inference, module scoring, donor-pseudobulk pathway enrichment, expression-based transcription-factor prioritization, co-expression analysis, ligand-target inference, and ARG1 virtual perturbation. We also quantified flow-gated bone marrow PMN-MDSCs and ARG1 protein in MOG35-55-induced EAE and tested systemic prophylactic oral nor-NOHA. MS bone marrow showed myeloid skewing and a heterogeneous PMN-MDSC-like transcriptional state, while donor-level subtype proportions were comparable between groups. Neutrophil degranulation showed the strongest BH-supported donor-pseudobulk enrichment, and expression-based regulatory and communication analyses converged on an ARG1-associated network. In EAE, flow-gated bone-marrow PMN-MDSCs and ARG1 protein were increased, and systemic prophylactic nor-NOHA was associated with lower clinical scores and reduced spinal-cord pathology. These data identify an ARG1-associated immunometabolic program in bone-marrow PMN-MDSC-like cells and connect the human transcriptional landscape with ARG1 protein expression and pharmacologic responses in EAE. Together, the findings establish ARG1-associated immunometabolism as a focused pathway for mechanistic and translational investigation.

title: Grey matter atrophy signatures and their genetic associations: a trans-disease study of Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and multiple sclerosis (MS) share neuroimmune mechanisms that drive neurodegeneration. Current clinical interventions are largely confined to a single-disease approach, owing to the absence of trans-disease diagnostic markers and common therapeutic targets. To map common and disease-specific grey matter (GM) atrophy patterns in AD and MS and identify their genetic correlations. We performed a trans-disease meta-analysis in large-sample neuroimaging data from 2001 to 2024 (2,070 MS versus 1,625 healthy control, and 1,624 AD versus 1,607 healthy control) to map GM atrophy regions. The cross-sample partial least squares regression was applied to integrate gene expression profiles from the Allen Human Brain Atlas with region-specific GM atrophy patterns, achieving cross-scale analysis of identify neurodegeneration-associated genes. MS-specific atrophy localized to the bilateral dorsomedial thalamic nucleus and precentral gyrus, whereas AD-specific atrophy centered on bilateral hippocampus-amygdala complex in age-unadjusted comparisons. The common atrophy patterns were found in the bilateral superior temporal gyrus, insulae, posterior cingulate cortex, amygdalae, and striatal components. We identified 834 genes whose spatial expression patterns were associated with the common GM atrophy pattern in AD and MS, including PLS2 + and PLS2- subsets, which encompass biological processes such as immunological homeostasis imbalance, cellular stress response, and neurometabolic/functional regulation. Findings establish shared cortical-limbic-striatal atrophy as pivotal neurodegeneration nexus in AD and MS. The identified gene-imaging signatures provide insights into potential pathway-specific mechanisms and may inform future therapeutic target discovery for dual-disease intervention.

title: Combining pharmacological and non-invasive brain stimulation strategies to promote remyelination in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Remyelination in multiple sclerosis (MS) fails for several, partly overlapping reasons. The differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells into myelin-producing oligodendrocytes is impaired both by intrinsic factors and by the surrounding lesion environment, which becomes increasingly inflammatory and senescent with age. Pharmacological strategies acting on a single target to promote oligodendrocyte lineage progression have been successful in animal models but have yet to produce meaningful clinical benefit in people with MS (pwMS). In this perspective paper, we argue that simultaneously targeting several of the mechanisms underlying this failure is a more promising route to repairing myelin lesions in pwMS. We outline how non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) might be leveraged to shift the glial microenvironment towards a pro-regenerative, remyelinating state, and how this can be paired with targeted pharmacological agents that enhance oligodendrocyte differentiation. We also discuss how the expected effect of such a combination may depend on age and lesion stage. This framework may offer a rational route beyond the translational failures of single-target remyelination therapies.

title: Neuron myelination is accelerated by Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibition via microglial extracellular vesicles.
abstract: The altered myelin repair observed in demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) potentially exposes axons to various stressors, with consequent neurodegeneration. Preclinical evidence has demonstrated that Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKi), such as ibrutinib, delay MS progression by acting on myeloid cells. We investigated the effects of ibrutinib on remyelination using a novel in vitro model of spinal cord neurons derived from postnatal mice. We demonstrated that (1) spinal cord neuron cells represent a suitable model for investigating myelination following L‑α‑lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) treatment; (2) ibrutinib induces remyelination and reduces stathmin‑1 expression in spinal cord cultures; and (3) ibrutinib reduces the inflammatory phenotype of microglia‑like BV2 cells, thereby modulating the expression of miR‑223 in extracellular vesicles (EVs). Altogether, these data pave the way for a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying remyelination following ibrutinib treatment and support the hypothesis that EV‑derived microglial cells play a key role.

title: Altered network organization with shift to local processing during adaptive behaviour in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: To adjust to changing environmental demands, the brain needs to organize and (re)configure mental resources in so-called task sets. Following a network perspective of cognitive functions, these processes are considered to rely on dynamic exchange of information between distant brain regions, possibly synchronized by slow-wave theta oscillations. However, few attempts have been made to describe the directional transfer of information in theta networks during behavioural adaptation. In the current study, we examined directed neural information transfer in 57 healthy individuals and 57 patients with multiple sclerosis with a focus on brain-behaviour associations during task switching. For this, we calculated behavioural switch costs and further applied an artificial neural network-based approach on neurophysiological EEG data to estimate linear and non-linear effective connectivity measures within cortical networks during task switching. Source reconstruction and connectivity analyses revealed distinct neural network architectures and communication strategies during task switching in healthy controls compared to patients with multiple sclerosis. In healthy controls, enhanced modulations of long-range fronto-parietal connectivities were associated with higher reaction time switch costs, possibly reflecting increased cognitive demands rather than adaptive processes. In contrast, patients with multiple sclerosis relied more strongly on local intra-regional modulations, which is consistent with the idea of a dysconnectivity syndrome in multiple sclerosis. Strikingly, stronger modulations in self-connectivities were associated with better accuracy measures in patients with multiple sclerosis, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to support performance. Notably, only non-linear directed connectivity measures were related to behavioural switch costs, emphasizing the importance of non-linear models for adaptive cognitive processes.

title: A 2-year multimodal prospective cohort study to predict sustained progression independent of relapse activity in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Disability accrual in multiple sclerosis (MS) is heterogeneous. We assessed whether a 2-year multimodal evaluation could identify patients who were developing progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) or relapse-associated worsening (RAW). Among the 81 MS patients with a 2-year follow-up and outcomes determined through 5 years, a composite for PIRA was developed using Firth's penalized logistic regression analysis; discrimination was calculated as the area under the curve (AUC) using repeated stratified nested cross-validation. In total, 21 patients (25.9%) met the PIRA criteria, 9 (11.1%) met the RAW criteria, and 1 met both criteria. A multivariate Firth regression analysis selected two variables associated with PIRA after adjustment: Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS) total score (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.17-3.83; A two-year multimodal assessment identified a biologically coherent PIRA composite driven by intrathecal neuroinflammation and fatigue. No reliable RAW predictor was found, and external validation is warranted.

title: Altered metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria contacts in multiple sclerosis neurons.
abstract: Genetic factors are estimated to account for approximately 30-50% of the risk for developing Multiple sclerosis (MS). Distinct mitochondrial variants, impairments in the respiratory chain, and mitochondrial dysfunction have been reported in individuals affected by MS. Mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) form membrane contact sites (ERMCs) that control important biological functions. Dysregulated ERMCs have been associated with a number of severe consequences for homeostasis, including altered mitochondrial calcium levels, impaired ATP production and abnormal lipid transfer. All of these mechanisms are thought to play an important role in the pathogenesis and disease progression of MS. Here, we investigated the hypothesis that the mitochondrial predisposition plays a crucial role in contributing to MS development. Mitochondrial functionality was analyzed in a model of human induced primary neurons (iPNs), and neuronal precursor cells (NPCs), differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from people with MS and healthy controls (HCs). Seahorse analysis was performed for investigation of the bioenergetic profile of the cells. ERMC and mitochondrial morphological analysis were carried out to investigate the potential impact of mitochondrial dysfunction in MS-derived neurons. Seahorse analysis revealed significant differences in the respiratory complexes (spare capacity: Our data are highlighting the importance of genetic mitochondrial contribution to MS pathology, by showing that MS-derived NPCs and iPNs exhibit altered mitochondrial behavior and morphology compared to healthy control (HC)-derived cells.

title: Fifteen-year real-world pharmacovigilance of multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: adverse event profiles, drug-specific safety signals and clinical implications.
abstract: Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) are the cornerstone of remission-phase management for multiple sclerosis (MS), a prevalent autoimmune neuroinflammatory disorder of the central nervous system. However, their immune-modulating mechanisms carry inherent risks of systemic and neurological adverse events (ADEs), which remain a major barrier to optimal long-term care. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the real-world safety profiles of all major MS DMT classes and identify clinically actionable safety signals. We analyzed 15-year (2009Q1-2023Q4) ADE reports for 8 classes of FDA-approved MS DMTs from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database. Four disproportionality algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were used for signal detection. Time-to-onset (TTO) analysis with Weibull distribution and multivariate logistic regression were performed to assess temporal risk patterns and patient-specific risk factors for important medical events (IMEs). A total of 498,847 ADE reports (1,048,575 events) were included, with nearly 50% involving IMEs. The most common ADEs were systemic symptoms, infections, liver injury and alopecia. Notably, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML, ROR = 15.59) and spontaneous abortion (ROR = 2.54) were identified as high-risk severe events. Drug-specific analysis revealed distinct safety signatures: anti-CD20 antibodies carried the highest infection risk, natalizumab was strongly associated with PML (ROR = 45.62), and teriflunomide had the highest alopecia risk (ROR = 12.73). Approximately 70% of IMEs occurred within 2 years of treatment initiation. Multivariate analysis identified older age, male sex and longer treatment duration as independent risk factors for IMEs, while obesity was a protective factor. This long-term FAERS-based analysis identified potential safety signals associated with major MS DMTs, providing hypothesis-generating evidence to support clinical vigilance and prioritize further validation, but not to estimate incidence, comparative risk, or causality.

title: Non-PML neuroinvasive infections reported with multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: a mechanism-based pharmacovigilance study, 2004-2025.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) alter host immunity and may produce pathogen-specific susceptibility to neuroinvasive infection. Comparative evidence is limited because events are rare and postmarketing research focuses mainly on progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). We analyzed deduplicated US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports from 2004Q1 to 2025Q4 using a prespecified case-non-case design. Tier A comprised direct high-certainty non-PML neuroinvasive infection terms. Tier B comprised a possible CNS infectious syndrome plus pathogen evidence elsewhere in the report, without CNS confirmation; tier A+B was a lower-certainty expanded endpoint for sensitivity and pathogen composition analyses. We estimated overall reporting (E1), pathogen composition within tier A+B (E2), and same-pathogen CNS localization (E3). Five DMT mechanisms were compared with contemporaneous active DMTs using calendar-year Mantel-Haenszel reporting odds ratios and covariate-adjusted Jeffreys-prior penalized logistic models. Among 492,514 reports, 675 were tier A and 82 additional reports were tier B. Tier A aRORs (95% CIs) were 0.82 (0.63-1.05) for anti-CD20 therapies, 1.77 (1.44-2.16) for S1P modulators, 1.32 (1.06-1.64) for natalizumab, 3.28 (2.24-4.66) for alemtuzumab, and 0.56 (0.21-1.19) for cladribine. Fingolimod accounted for 145 of 152 S1P cases and had an aROR of 2.15 (1.75-2.64). Among four mechanisms eligible for E2, pathogen composition differed (LRT 210.59, 9 E1 contrasts were interpreted as separate reporting comparisons, not a formal equality test across mechanisms. S1P reporting was largely fingolimod-driven, and natalizumab-HSV/VZV was the only prespecified pair with adjusted same-pathogen CNS enrichment. Findings support targeted vigilance and confirmatory studies but do not estimate incidence or establish causality.

title: Seizures and epilepsy in MOG antibody-associated disease: from cortical neuroimmunology to clinical practice.
abstract: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder distinct from multiple sclerosis (MS) and aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4-NMOSD). Seizures are an important but incompletely characterized manifestation. Their reported prevalence is strongly age-dependent-approximately 30% in pediatric-onset versus 7% in adult-onset cohorts, although these estimates are influenced by referral and publication bias-and clusters around cerebral cortical encephalitis (CCE) and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in anti-MOG-associated encephalitis with seizures (FLAMES). This raises a mechanistic question: why is cortical MOGAD particularly ictogenic, and how does demyelination interact with lesion anatomy and inflammatory composition to promote cortical hyperexcitability? This review places the neuroimmunology of MOGAD-related seizures at its center. We summarize the epidemiology, age gradient and clinical spectrum-CCE/FLAMES, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)-associated seizures, isolated sentinel seizures, status epilepticus, new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE), and MOG-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) overlap-together with the distinction between acute symptomatic seizures and autoimmune-associated epilepsy. We then examine MOG-IgG effector biology, the CD4+ T-cell- and macrophage-predominant pathology, B-cell compartmentalization, the meningo-cortical axis, and the Th17/interleukin-6-weighted cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) milieu. Candidate downstream pathways of inflammatory ictogenesis are presented with an explicit separation between MOGAD-specific associations and mechanisms extrapolated from epilepsy. Finally, we translate this framework into differential diagnosis, assay interpretation, electroencephalographic evaluation, immunotherapy-first management, antiseizure medication (ASM) review, neuropsychological follow-up and testable research priorities.

title: Is resistance training effective to increase BDNF in multiple sclerosis? An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of isolated interventions.
abstract: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key mediator of neuroplasticity and has been associated with disease progression in multiple sclerosis (MS). While aerobic exercise is consistently linked to BDNF modulation, the specific contribution of isolated resistance training (RT) remains unclear, as previous reviews have largely combined multimodal exercise interventions. To systematically review and meta-analyze the effects of isolated RT on peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS (PROSPERO: CRD420251141069). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scielo, Scopus, PEDro and Cochrane up to January 10, 2026, using PICOT criteria. Controlled experimental studies investigating isolated RT and BDNF outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Due to methodological heterogeneity, a random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled effects. Four studies (three RCTs and one controlled non-randomized trial), totaling 126 participants with MS, were included. Interventions lasted 8-24 weeks, with training frequencies of 2-3 sessions per week. Meta-analytic synthesis revealed positive pooled effects (SMD = 0.49; 95%CI: 0.15 to 0.83; Z = 2.80; p < 0.005; I2  = 0%; Q = 1.681) with wide confidence intervals without crossing zero. With the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, due to the reduced number of studies, the analysis continued to show a positive intervention effect: (SMD = 0.49; 95%CI: 0.42 to 0.56; t = 3.716; p = 0.0339). Two studies using low-to-moderate intensity protocols (Pilates-based RT and low-load RT with bands/weights) showed significant increases in serum BDNF after 8 weeks. In contrast, studies employing higher loads (≈80% of one-repetition maximum: 1RM) demonstrated no significant BDNF changes despite functional gains. Overall certainty of evidence was rated as low due to risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Isolated RT may increase peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS, but this effect is supported by limited and low-certainty evidence. Furthermore, given that only four studies were included in the meta-analysis, we suggest interpreting the results with some caution.

title: CAR-T-cell therapy for autoimmune neurologic diseases.
abstract: Autoimmune neurologic diseases include multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, autoimmune encephalitis, myasthenia gravis, stiff-person syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, and related syndromes. The contributions of B cells, plasma cells, and autoantibodies differ substantially across these disorders; however, the B-cell lineage represents a therapeutically actionable target in many of them. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, originally developed for hematologic malignancies, offers a potential strategy for deep and potentially durable depletion of pathogenic B-lineage cells and subsequent immune reconstitution. In recent years, CD19, BCMA, dual-target, mRNA CAR-T-cell, and chimeric autoantibody receptor T-cell approaches have generated preliminary clinical or translational evidence, primarily in systemic autoimmune diseases. Clinical evidence in neurologic disorders remains limited and spans myasthenia gravis, NMOSD, MOGAD, multiple sclerosis, autoimmune encephalitis, stiff-person syndrome, and CIDP. This review summarizes the biologic rationale, disease-specific evidence, target selection, safety concerns, and trial-design considerations for CAR-T-cell therapy in autoimmune neurologic diseases. Current evidence supports further investigation of CAR-T cells in selected patients with highly refractory, antibody- or B-cell-driven neuroimmune disorders, but does not establish superiority over existing therapies. However, the field remains dominated by case reports and small early-phase studies, with randomized evidence currently confined to one phase 2b trial in myasthenia gravis. Establishing the risk-benefit profile will require stringent patient selection, disease-specific neurologic monitoring, controlled prospective studies, and long-term follow-up.

title: Perception of virus effects and vaccination among people with multiple sclerosis in Saudi Arabia.
abstract: BACKGROUND: People with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) are at increased risk of infection due to immune dysregulation and exposure to disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). Despite this risk, real-world vaccine uptake remains inconsistent. This study evaluated vaccination readiness, counseling practices, and infection-related perceptions among pwMS in Saudi Arabia. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among adults with MS (n = 204) recruited using non-probability (convenience) sampling from tertiary-care clinical and community-based sources. The survey assessed demographic characteristics, vaccination attitudes and uptake, counseling experiences, perceptions of infection risk related to MS and DMTs, and awareness of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Internal consistency of multi-item measures was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.72). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize outcomes. RESULTS: The cohort was relatively young (mean age 35.7 years), with two-thirds aged 25-44 years (25-34 years: 38.2%; 35-44 years: 36.8%). Most participants held a bachelor's degree (66.7%). Attitudes toward routine vaccination were frequently non-committal: 47.6% were somewhat or very likely to vaccinate, 33.8% were neutral, and 18.6% were somewhat or very unlikely; separately, 60.8% agreed or somewhat agreed that routine vaccines might be harmful for pwMS. COVID-19 vaccination uptake was high (72.5%), whereas influenza vaccination was low (30.9%). Uptake of other adult vaccines, including hepatitis B, meningococcal, herpes zoster, and human papillomavirus vaccines, was < 10% for each. Perceived infection vulnerability was substantial, with 62.7% expressing concern about viral infections due to MS and 71.1% believing that DMTs increased susceptibility, consistent with 59.4% receiving high-efficacy DMTs. Awareness of EBV was limited: 26.5% had heard of EBV, 16.6% perceived an MS-EBV association, and 21.1% were aware of possible causality. Nearly half of participants (49.0%) were undecided about a hypothetical EBV vaccine, while approximately 44% expressed willingness to receive it. Counseling gaps were evident, as only 32.8% reported any discussion about vaccination with clinicians; counseling prior to DMT initiation and during ongoing treatment was reported by 16.2% and 19.1%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In a young and highly educated cohort of pwMS in Saudi Arabia, vaccine hesitancy and counseling gaps persist despite high perceived infection risk. These findings highlight the need for structured and routine vaccine counseling, particularly at MS diagnosis and before initiating high-efficacy DMTs, to improve uptake of influenza and other recommended adult vaccines in MS clinics.

title: Epstein-Barr virus shapes intrathecal Th1/Th17 immunity and parenchymal involvement in neuro-Behçet's disease.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Human herpesviruses (HHVs) are implicated in neuro-inflammatory diseases due to their ability to establish persistent latency and reactivate in the context of immune dysregulation. Whilst Epstein -Barr virus (EBV) is recognized as a key factor in multiple sclerosis (MS), its role in neuro-Behçet's disease (NBD) remains poorly understood. METHODS: Serum and paired CSF samples were obtained from treatment-naïve patients with NBD and MS. Neurotropic viral DNA in CSF was screened by multiplex PCR. Virus-specific IgG antibodies against HSV-1 and EBV antigens (VCA and EBNA1) were measured by ELISA in serum and CSF. Real-time PCR was used to assess the expression of EBV latent genes (LMP1 and EBNA1), as well as cytokines and transcription factors, in CSF samples from NBD patients. RESULTS: In this study, we demonstrate a high prevalence of EBV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NBD (71.43%), significantly higher than that observed in MS (35.29%), whereas other neurotropic herpesviruses are rarely detected. Notably, the presence of EBV in the CSF is not associated with a specific intrathecal humoral response, suggesting predominantly latent viral persistence and cell-mediated immune control. The concurrent expression of the latent proteins LMP1 and EBNA1 indicates a type II latency program, capable of activating interferon pathways. EBV-positive patients exhibit an immune signature characterized by significantly elevated levels of IFN-γ and IFN-α, associated with Th1/Th17 polarization and reduced FOXP3 expression, reflecting a Th17/Treg imbalance. Furthermore, EBV status is associated with distinct clinical phenotypes, with parenchymal forms being observed exclusively in EBV-positive patients. CONCLUSION: This suggests that EBV may contribute to the pathophysiology of NBD by promoting a pro-inflammatory intrathecal microenvironment. It also positions EBV as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target in this condition.

title: B-Cell-Related Neuroinflammation Across Central Nervous System Diseases: A Bibliometric and Science-Mapping Analysis, 2006-2026.
abstract: PURPOSE: Research on B cells in central nervous system (CNS) diseases rests on a mature multiple sclerosis (MS) literature, whereas evidence in CNS injury and neurodegeneration is still emerging. We mapped publications from 2006 to 2026 and separated bibliometric visibility from mechanistic maturity. METHODS: We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) on August 17, 2026, for English-language records carrying the Article document-type tag and published from January 1, 2006, through August 17, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened all records, with unresolved disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer. Publication trends, collaboration, co-citation, journal flows, citation bursts, and keyword evolution were analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, bibliometrix, R, and SCImago Graphica. Search materials, parameters, and source tables were archived. RESULTS: After database-level limits, 2,701 records were screened; 467 (17.3%) were excluded and 2,234 (82.7%) included. The corpus had accrued 91,218 WoSCC citations. Annual output rose from 91 articles in 2016 to 231 in 2025; 173 articles from 2026 represent a partial year. The United States contributed the most articles, and the University of California, San Francisco ranked first after affiliation normalization. Co-citation and keyword analyses showed an MS/experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-centered foundation built around B-cell depletion trials, meningeal pathology, diagnostic criteria, and regulatory B-cell biology. Recent bursts included anti-CD20 therapy, single-cell RNA sequencing, autoimmune encephalitis, ischemic stroke, Mendelian randomization, B-cell depletion, and Alzheimer disease. CONCLUSION: B-cell-related CNS research has expanded, but evidence maturity remains disease-specific. MS/EAE provides the clearest foundation. Findings in CNS injury, neurodegeneration, and candidate peripheral-CNS routes remain context-dependent and require validation by disease, anatomical compartment, B-cell state, and stage. Bibliometric prominence reveals attention, not shared causality or therapeutic efficacy.

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. METHODS: Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. RESULTS: Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. DISCUSSION: Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.

title: Cellular senescence in multiple sclerosis: hallmarks, immunosenescence, and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated neurodegenerative disease where chronological aging predicts the conversion to progressive MS (PMS), a phase defined by compartmentalized inflammation and accelerated neurodegeneration. While current disease modifying therapies (DMTs) are effective for managing the inflammatory aspect of MS, treatments remain inadequate. It is imperative to understand the biology of aging including an important hallmark of aging, cellular senescence. Cellular senescence is a state of cell cycle arrest where cells remain in their senescent state and produce a distinctive senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), characterized by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors. Growing experimental and clinical evidence suggests that the accumulation of senescent cells and SASP secretion perpetuates a pathological feedback loop linking age-related processes with accelerated neurodegeneration observed in PMS. Whether senescence drives PMS or accompanies it remains unresolved. In this Review, we outline the biology of aging, senescence pathway markers, and SASP components. We evaluate studies of cellular senescence and SASP markers in MS, including immunosenescence, T- and B-cell changes; the contributions of Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus-1; and the relationship between senescence burden, brain atrophy, and DMT response. Lastly, we outline the available senotherapeutic approaches aimed at mitigating MS and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Targeting TLR4 alleviates the progression of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis by regulating central resident cells and Th1/Th17 cell differentiation.

title: Thalamic atrophy in active and inactive secondary progressive multiple sclerosis patients: A comparative study.
abstract: Thalamic atrophy may be an indicator of neurodegeneration in people with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (pwSPMS). The atrophy usually begins asymmetrically, and the thalamic asymmetry index (TAI) can be used to estimate the severity of neurodegeneration. SPMS is commonly divided into two groups of active and inactive. No study has compared TAI between SPMS groups and examine its relationships with cognitive and motor measures in pwSPMS. This study aimed to compare the TAI between active and inactive pwSPMS and to examine its relationship with key clinical, cognitive, and motor variables. In this cross-sectional study, 38 pwSPMS (15 active and 23 inactive) were enrolled from February to November 2024. MRI-based volumetric measurements were used to determine thalamic volumes and calculate the TAI. Cognitive and motor tests, including the SDMT, PASAT, and 9HPT were also administered alongside clinical examinations. Active SPMS patients had significantly lower NTV compared to inactive patients (Cohen's d = -1.58, p < 0.001). No significant difference in TAI was observed between groups. NTV correlated with cognitive scores in both active (r = 0.74, P = 0.002) and inactive (r = 0.65, p < 0.001) groups and with disability in the inactive group (r = -0.5, P= 0.014). Active SPMS patients showed worse cognitive and motor performance. Thalamic atrophy is more severe in active SPMS and is associated with worse cognitive and motor outcomes. While thalamic asymmetry did not differentiate between subgroups, it may serve as a marker for functional status in SPMS.

title: Review Article: A Scientific Journey with Zelig Eshhar at the Dawn of Monoclonal Antibody Research.
abstract: Professor Zelig Eshhar, a colleague, collaborator, and dear friend, is known worldwide as the visionary who laid the foundations for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, a breakthrough that transformed cancer immunotherapy. Long before this revolutionary achievement, however, Zelig profoundly influenced research at the Weizmann Institute of Science by introducing the then state-of-the-art hybridoma technology for the generation of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which he brought directly from the oven of Nobel laureates Georges KÃ¶hler and CÃ©sar Milstein. Through his expertise and the dedication of his legendary team, Tova Waks, his indispensable partner for 55 years, Orith Gigi-Leitner, and Sara Barak, this technology rapidly became an invaluable resource for investigators throughout the Institute. My collaboration with Zelig during the 1980s led to the generation of monoclonal antibodies against a series of biologically important proteins, including interferons, other cytokines, their soluble receptors, the unique IL-18 Binding Protein (IL-18BP), and, years later, glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase 1 (GOT1). These antibodies proved to be remarkably versatile research tools, suitable for neutralization, affinity chromatography, immunoassays, flow cytometry, immunoblotting, and numerous other applications. Most importantly, they enabled the affinity purification of in-house corresponding recombinant cytokines. The antibodies proved far more than analytical reagents. They became indispensable tools for both basic research and translational medicine. Together, these unique reagents formed the foundation of a ligand-affinity strategy that led to the discovery of previously unknown cytokine receptors and binding proteins. Those include the type I interferon receptor, the second TNF receptor (TBPII), and the unexpected IL-18 Binding Protein. These discoveries not only advanced our understanding of cytokine biology but also paved the way for therapeutics such as RebifŴ, EnbrelŴ, RemicadeŴ and Tadekinig alfaTM, used in the treatment of autoimmune, inflammatory, and genetic diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. While our scientific paths diverged in 1989, Zelig's toward the revolutionary concept of chimeric antigen receptors and mine toward cytokine receptors and binding proteins, they ultimately converged again as TNF and IL-18BP antagonists found applications in enhancement of CAR-T therapy and in management of potential inflammatory complications associated with this therapy. This chapter stands as a testament to Zelig's vision in introducing and advancing monoclonal antibody technology at the Weizmann Institute.
